definitions.definition: CYCLE — One complete set of positive and negative values of an alternating quantity is a cycle. One cycle of alternating voltage corresponds to 360° or 2π radians.

sourceReferences.sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf

definitions.definition: TIME PERIOD — The time in seconds to complete one cycle of an alternating quantity is its time period, generally represented by T.

sourceReferences.sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf

definitions.definition: FREQUENCY — The number of cycles per second is frequency f, measured in cycles per second or hertz (Hz). Pakistan’s power-system frequency is 50 Hz, meaning alternating voltage or current completes 50 cycles each second.

sourceReferences.sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf

definitions.definition: INSTANTANEOUS VALUE — The value of an alternating quantity at any instant is its instantaneous value. Instantaneous alternating voltage and current are represented by V and I, respectively.

sourceReferences.sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf

definitions.definition: PEAK VALUE — The maximum value attained by an A.C. waveform is its peak value, also called maximum value or amplitude. Peak alternating voltage and current are represented by Vₘ and Iₘ, respectively.

sourceReferences.sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf

definitions.definition: AVERAGE VALUE — The average of all waveform values over a period of time. For an interval, add the values and divide by the time; treat area above the time axis as positive and area below as negative, using algebraic signs for total net area. Average value of A.C. = total net area under the curve for time T / time T.

sourceReferences.sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf

definitions.definition: R.M.S. OR EFFECTIVE VALUE — The r.m.s. value of an alternating current is the steady D.C. current that produces the same heat in a resistor as the alternating current does in the same resistance for the same time. The r.m.s. or effective value is used to express the magnitude of alternating current or voltage.

sourceReferences.sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf

definitions.definition: The phase of a particular amplitude is the fraction of a time period or cycle through which the quantity has progressed from a selected zero reference. “Phasor” is short for phase vector; it represents a sine or cosine function graphically.

sourceReferences.sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf

definitions.definition: PHASE DIFFERENCE — Two or more A.C. voltages or currents may have waveforms that are not synchronized: their peaks and zero points do not coincide at the same times. When two alternating quantities of the same frequency have different zero points, they have a phase difference. The quantity that crosses zero earlier is leading; the other is lagging. The text next compares I and V waves with the same amplitude and frequency but different phase.

workedExamples.title: Example 15.1 — pure resistive A.C. circuit
workedExamples.question: EXAMPLE 15.1 — A pure 20 Ω resistance is connected across a 220 V, 50 Hz A.C. supply. Calculate (a) current, (b) power consumed, and (c) equations for voltage and current. GIVEN: f = 50 Hz, R = 20 Ω, V = 220 V. REQUIRED: I, P and voltage/current equations.
workedExamples.solution: SOLUTION — Vₘ = √2V = √2 × 220 = 311.1 V. (a) I = V/R = 220/20 = 11 A. (b) Average power P = VI = 220 × 11 = 2420 W. Iₘ = √2I = 15.55 A and ω = 2πf = 314 rad s⁻¹. (c) V = 311.1 sin(314t) and I = 15.55 sin(314t).

workedExamples.title: Example 15.2 — pure inductive coil
workedExamples.question: EXAMPLE 15.2 — A pure inductive coil draws 20 A from a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. Find (1) inductive reactance, (2) coil inductance, (3) power absorbed, and the voltage/current equations. GIVEN: I = 20 A, V = 220 V, f = 50 Hz.
workedExamples.solution: SOLUTION — Xₗ = V/I = 220/20 = 11 Ω. Since Xₗ = 2πfL, L = Xₗ/(2πf) = 11/(2π × 50) = 0.035 H. Power absorbed P = 0. Vₘ = 220√2 = 311.1 V; Iₘ = 20√2 = 28.28 A; ω = 2π × 50 = 314 rad s⁻¹. In a pure inductive circuit current lags voltage by π/2: V = 311.1 sin(314t) V; I = 28.28 sin(314t − π/2) A.

workedExamples.title: Example 15.3 — voltage across an inductor
workedExamples.question: EXAMPLE 15.3 GIVEN — Inductance L = 60 mH; current I = 0.2 sin(377t − 25°) A. REQUIRED — Write the mathematical expression for voltage V across the inductor. SOLUTION — Xₗ = 2πfL = 377 × 60 × 10⁻³ = 22.62 Ω. Vₘ = IₘXₗ = 0.2 × 22.62 = 4.5 V. Voltage leads current by 90°, so add 90° to its phase: V = Vₘ sin(377t − 25° + 90°) = 4.5 sin(377t + 65°) V.

workedExamples.title: Example 15.4 — capacitor across 220 V, 50 Hz
workedExamples.question: EXAMPLE 15.4 — A 318 μF capacitor is connected across a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. Find (1) capacitive reactance, (2) r.m.s. current, and the equations for voltage and current. GIVEN: C = 318 μF = 318 × 10⁻⁶ F; f = 50 Hz; V = 220 V. SOLUTION: Xc = 1/(2πfC) = 1/[2π × 50 × (318 × 10⁻⁶)] = 10.26 Ω. I = V/Xc = 220/10.26 = 21.44 A. Vm = 220√2 = 311.1 V; Im = 21.44√2 = 30.32 A; ω = 2π × 50 = 314 (source prints unit Hz). Thus V = 311.1 sin314t V and, since current leads voltage by 90°, I = 30.32 sin(314t + π/2) A.

workedExamples.title: Example 15.5 — R–L coil on 220 V, 50 Hz
workedExamples.question: EXAMPLE 15.5 — A coil with resistance 7 Ω and inductance 31.8 mH is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. Find circuit current, phase angle, power factor and power consumed. GIVEN: L = 31.8 mH; V = 220 V; R = 7 Ω; f = 50 Hz. SOLUTION: X_L = 2πfL = 2π×50×31.8×10⁻³ = 10 Ω. Z = √(R²+X_L²) = √(7²+10²) = 12.2 Ω. I = V/Z = 220/12.2 = 18.03 A. tanφ = X_L/R = 10/7; φ = tan⁻¹(10/7) = 55° lag. Power factor cos55° = 0.573 lag. P = VI cosφ = 220×18.03×0.573 = 2272.8 W.
workedExamples.solution: EXAMPLE 15.5 — A coil with resistance 7 Ω and inductance 31.8 mH is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. Find circuit current, phase angle, power factor and power consumed. GIVEN: L = 31.8 mH; V = 220 V; R = 7 Ω; f = 50 Hz. SOLUTION: X_L = 2πfL = 2π×50×31.8×10⁻³ = 10 Ω. Z = √(R²+X_L²) = √(7²+10²) = 12.2 Ω. I = V/Z = 220/12.2 = 18.03 A. tanφ = X_L/R = 10/7; φ = tan⁻¹(10/7) = 55° lag. Power factor cos55° = 0.573 lag. P = VI cosφ = 220×18.03×0.573 = 2272.8 W.
workedExamples.answer: I = 18.03 A; φ = 55° lag; power factor = 0.573 lag; P = 2272.8 W

workedExamples.title: Example 15.6 — series capacitor and resistor
workedExamples.question: EXAMPLE 15.6 — A 100 V, 50 Hz A.C. supply is applied to a 79.5 μF capacitor in series with a non-inductive 30 Ω resistor. Find impedance, current, phase angle and instantaneous-current equation. GIVEN: V = 100 V; R = 30 Ω; f = 50 Hz; C = 79.5 μF. SOLUTION: X_C = 1/(2πfC) = 40 Ω. Z = √(R²+X_C²) = √(30²+40²) = 50 Ω. I = V/Z = 100/50 = 2 A. tanφ = X_C/R = 40/30 = 1.33, so φ = tan⁻¹(1.33) = 53° lead. I_m = I√2 = 2.828 A; ω = 2πf = 314 rad s⁻¹. Thus I_inst = 2.828 sin(314t + 53°) A.
workedExamples.solution: EXAMPLE 15.6 — A 100 V, 50 Hz A.C. supply is applied to a 79.5 μF capacitor in series with a non-inductive 30 Ω resistor. Find impedance, current, phase angle and instantaneous-current equation. GIVEN: V = 100 V; R = 30 Ω; f = 50 Hz; C = 79.5 μF. SOLUTION: X_C = 1/(2πfC) = 40 Ω. Z = √(R²+X_C²) = √(30²+40²) = 50 Ω. I = V/Z = 100/50 = 2 A. tanφ = X_C/R = 40/30 = 1.33, so φ = tan⁻¹(1.33) = 53° lead. I_m = I√2 = 2.828 A; ω = 2πf = 314 rad s⁻¹. Thus I_inst = 2.828 sin(314t + 53°) A.
workedExamples.answer: Z = 50 Ω; I = 2 A; φ = 53° lead; I_inst = 2.828 sin(314t + 53°) A

workedExamples.title: Example 15.7 — series R–L–C circuit
workedExamples.question: EXAMPLE 15.7 — A 220 V, 50 Hz A.C. supply is applied to a coil of inductance 0.06 H and resistance 2.5 Ω in series with a 6.8 μF capacitor. Find impedance, current, phase angle, power factor and power. GIVEN: L=0.06 H; R=2.5 Ω; V=220 V; f=50 Hz; C=6.8 μF. SOLUTION: X_L=2πfL=18.85 Ω; X_C=1/(2πfC)=468 Ω. Z=√[R²+(X_L−X_C)²]=449.2 Ω. I=V/Z=0.4897 A. tanφ=(X_L−X_C)/R=−179.66, so φ=−89.7° and current leads voltage. Power factor cosφ=R/Z=0.00557. P=VI cosφ=220×0.4897×0.00557=0.60007 W.
